questions.question: What did the group discuss about the trend of teacher recruiting and the reasons for it, and steps they had taken?
questions.reference_answer: Although there were no exact figures,they had seen over recent years that they were only recruiting to about 65 percent of targets. It was partially due to the financial incentives, but that was not all of the problems. Because this issue was not only in Wales, but a common issue in all over the world. For example, in England, despite higher financial incentives to join ITE courses, people still were not getting onto those courses. To solve this problem, they had taken several steps including making sure their ITE provision was world class, embarking on the first national ITE recruitment marketing exercise, etc. In this process, Llyr Gruffydd had a doubt that the level of ambition did not reflect the level of action that was needed actually. Kirsty Williams responded that different statistics told different stories. They obviously understood there were many steps they had to take, but they were trying instead of just sitting back and waiting.

oracle.answer:
The group discussed the trend of teacher recruiting, noting that they are only recruiting to about 65% of their targets for priority subjects. They highlighted that this issue is not unique to Wales but is a global problem, with significant teacher shortages observed in various countries like the USA, England, Finland, and Australia. 

To address the issue, the group mentioned several steps they have taken:
1. Ensuring that Initial Teacher Education (ITE) provision is of high quality.
2. Offering financial incentives, particularly for graduates with top qualifications in priority subjects, up to £20,000 annually.
3. Launching a national ITE recruitment marketing campaign, targeting Welsh students studying priority subjects.
4. Increasing employment-based routes into Qualified Teacher Status (QTS), with high demand for these positions.
5. Introducing a unique part-time PGCE route to allow individuals to combine employment with learning.
6. Setting up an advisory board under Professor John Gardner to understand the issues preventing people from entering the teaching profession.
7. Implementing new financial incentives for Welsh-medium teaching qualifications.
8. Working with ITE centers to develop minimum Welsh language skill requirements for all teachers.

They acknowledged that the problem is multifaceted and requires a combination of strategies to attract and retain teachers. Additionally, they noted the importance of increasing diversity in the teaching workforce, including encouraging career changers and those with diverse experiences to enter the profession.

Kirsty Williams thought there would be a responsibility upon the University of South Wales to ensure that those students already in the system were able to complete their studies with the appropriate level of support and tuition to enable them to achieve their career aspirations and graduate from that program.
